page.text:
Geometrically, complex conjugation $z \mapsto \overline{z}$ is the
reflection of the Argand plane across the real horizontal axis,
preserving distances and magnitudes while reversing planar orientation
and the sign of angles.

Algebraically, conjugation is a non-trivial field automorphism of
$\mathbb{C}$ that fixes every real number pointwise: $\sigma(x) = x$ for
all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, and $\sigma(i) = -i$. Because
$\sigma^2 = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{C}}$, conjugation is an
involution, generating the two-element Galois group
$\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
In particular, if a polynomial $P(z) \in \mathbb{R}[z]$ has real
coefficients, then $P(\overline{z}) = \overline{P(z)}$, which guarantees
that all non-real roots of real polynomials must occur in complex
conjugate pairs.
